served.stem: As used in paragraph 9, "blunt" most nearly means
choices: slow to take effect in the body
not sharp enough to cut tissue
served.bankWhy: The next sentence in paragraph 9 explains the word: MAC describes a population rather than the patient on the table, and it measures only whether a body moves. That is a measure too coarse to separate cases.

proof.quote: It describes a population rather than the patient on the table
the only thing it measures is whether a body moves

passage.title: Why Anaesthesia Still Lacks an Explanation

distractorNotes: Nothing suggests the measure has eroded over time. It is coarse from the start.
That is the everyday sense of blunt applied to speech, and here the word is judging a measurement.
Speed of onset is not what the sentence weighs. It weighs how much MAC can tell you.
The literal edge of a blade has no place here, since the word describes a criterion.

choiceTexts: slow to take effect in the body
not sharp enough to cut tissue

difficulty.from: question type (vocabulary in context); the RC bank has no difficulty field

answer.line: The next sentence defines it: MAC describes a population, not the patient on the table, and measures only whether a body moves.

steps: Read the sentence after the word. That is where the author explains "blunt".
Sentence 6: MAC "describes a population rather than the patient on the table", and it measures only whether a body moves.
So blunt means coarse. It cannot draw fine lines between patients, or between effects.

choices.note: A real sense of blunt, like a knife dulled by use. But nothing says MAC wore down; it was coarse from the start.
A population, and only movement: a measure too coarse for fine distinctions.
Blunt speech is a real sense, but MAC is a measure, not a remark.

choices.text: slow to take effect in the body
choices.note: Nothing in paragraph 9 is about how fast anything acts. The sentence after the word is about what MAC can tell you.

choices.text: not sharp enough to cut tissue
choices.note: The skin being cut in sentence 2 pulls toward a literal blade, but MAC is a number, not an instrument.

student.lockIt: Vocabulary in context: the sentence right after the word often defines it. Use that, not the dictionary sense.
